title: The Loud Liker Theory
author: Sahil Bloom
summary: Sahil Bloom explains why building new adult relationships is hard for people who are not natural in social settings, using two psychology findings. Signal Amplification Bias shows that people afraid of rejection overestimate how obviously they convey interest, while the Liking Gap shows that people systematically underestimate how much their conversation partner likes them. Together they mean you send less than you think and hear less than was sent, so two people who like each other can leave convinced the other does not. His remedy, borrowed from Vanessa Van Edwards, is the Loud Liker Theory: say your admiration out loud. He gives concrete habits such as complimenting a stranger, calling instead of texting, and sending notes of kudos, and credits them with new friendships and even a story idea for his second book. The asymmetric bet is a small risk of rejection for a large upside in connection.
points: Fear of rejection makes people overestimate how clear their social signals are, a pattern known as Signal Amplification Bias.
The Liking Gap means people consistently underestimate how much others like them, so warmth goes unrecognised on both sides.
The two effects compound, leaving mutually interested people each convinced the other is not, which stops relationships before they start.
Voicing admiration through compliments, quick calls and notes of kudos is a low-cost habit that closes the gap.
Adult friendships rarely come from sticky settings like school or teams, so they must be created deliberately by the person willing to go first.
quotes: The collision of these two scientific findings is painful. In effect, you send less than you think, and you hear less than they send. Two people who like each other leave an interaction convinced the other one doesn’t.
In simple terms, our fear of rejection in social situations tempers our ability to convey social signals, and blinds our ability to recognize that tempering effect.

Across multiple, diverse contexts, researchers found that people systematically underestimate their conversation partner’s liking for them. Third party observers accurately estimated how much each party liked the other, but participants themselves were blind to it.
Researchers believe it’s driven by our own self-critical internal monologue, paired with a natural egocentric bias that overemphasizes our own flaws.
If I admire something someone did, I send them a message to let them know. Big or small, it doesn’t matter.
In Vanessa’s words, “Being a loud liker costs you the occasional rejection and buys you nearly everything else.
My mom was a loud liker on my behalf 30 years ago. But as an adult, nobody’s going to do that for you.
